title: The AI Safety Coalition Suddenly Takes Shape, but Nobody Knows How to Measure the "Frontier"
dek: The Hugging Face incident brought the left and the AI safety camp together for the first time, but "pacing the frontier" is itself unmeasurable — with no legislation, third-party evaluation is just voluntary goodwill.
why: Medium information density: the first half hour on coalition politics and the second half hour on China's open-source cadence are the substance; the middle discussion of how evaluation outfits actually get off the ground wanders.
who: Founders and investors watching where AI regulation is heading, especially those who want to know how the US safety coalition took shape and whether China's open-source cadence will be interrupted.
skip: 47:14 to 50:18, the idle chat about Sam Altman movie casting and actors — skippable.

points.h: Anti-data-center and AI safety have merged
points.body: Jasmine's timeline: the early-August pacing open letter, then the Hugging Face incident right after — two threads colliding. Before this, anti-data-center, anti-AI populist sentiment was diffuse, and the AI safety crowd kept agonizing over whether to talk to people like Tucker Carlson and Bernie — worried the other side wasn't "truth-seeking." In the end the left dropped its suspicion of AI safety first; Bernie convinced the public more than anyone that "AI is real, AI risk is real," not corporate marketing spin. So when Hugging Face hit, the public was ready to care about real frontier safety issues.

points.h: The public doesn't care about extinction, but cares about companies out of control
points.body: Jasmine's judgment: nobody votes on AI issues, it doesn't even make the top five. But "these companies are too lawless, power is too concentrated, data centers need regulation, we need transparency, we need government audits" is a very widespread intuition. Ask the public whether they want third-party evaluators, whether they want to fund Casey — nobody has an opinion; but say AI has gone off the rails and the FBI should investigate, and everyone nods. Nathan added: the Hugging Face incident was narratively too smooth — a New York Post cover with the Terminator wouldn't even be a stretch; the rhyme of the facts happened to line up with a fear ordinary people can understand.

points.h: Alignment is temporary, cybersecurity is permanent
points.body: Nathan splits the problem in two: on differentiated frontier capabilities there really is an alignment responsibility, but a hole punched by a frontier lab will, in three to six months, be doable by three models, and in a year by twenty-plus organizations. So the alignment problem only "temporarily" belongs to frontier labs, whereas the cybersecurity problem won't go away on its own until it's actually solved. He also says people in the security world are clear: our infrastructure isn't ready for the tools that are about to be everywhere.

points.h: The word "pacing" is itself a self-interested choice
points.body: Jordan points out pacing is neither pause nor slowdown; choosing that word already implies still moving forward. Nathan is more direct: we simply don't know how to measure frontier models, and any pacing presupposes you can measure. What really bothers him is the in-lab rhetoric — "you can't see it, we're scared of the pace of progress internally too" — which is meaningless absent transparency. The mechanism he envisions: in every lab there's a group of people who can see one or two labs at once, jointly agreeing that the safety work for current capabilities is already sufficient.

points.h: Trust only exists between people who've known each other five years
points.body: Jasmine names the real obstacle to evaluation outfits getting off the ground: the reason Anthropic is willing to give METR people Slack access is that it's known them personally for five-plus years — trust at the level of "A.J. or Ryan Greenblatt can come in" — and that trust may not transfer to other METR people or other organizations. The second problem, raised by Jordan: if a third-party evaluator disagrees with the giant the US economy depends on, whose word does the government take? She also thinks third-party evaluation is actually a more AI-progress-friendly compromise than "the Trump administration sending people to shut down models at the door."

points.h: Without legislation, evaluation is just voluntary goodwill
points.body: Jasmine's conclusion is hard: as long as there's no legislation, everything is voluntary, so METR, Redwood and outfits like them will to some degree avoid angering the organization that grants them voluntary access. She cites METR and Redwood's investigation of the Hugging Face incident — entirely voluntary, they got only seven days of Slack logs, everyone wanted more, but at the time no legislation required OpenAI to do anything; it rested purely on them happening to trust these three random people. She also imagines a worse future: XAI, Anthropic and OpenAI are all pacing, Meta isn't, evaluators find the same fatal failure mode at all three, but that's each lab's private information, and Meta just YOLOs it out.

points.h: Chinese labs are climbing the hill, not switching paradigms
points.body: Nathan's judgment: within the current paradigm, Chinese labs are organized to be very good at hill climbing. Zhipu and ZAI's post-training stack is already mature, GLM 5.2 and 5.3 are both solid, Kimi's base model recipe is figured out, and what they're doing is scaling RL environments, scaling RL, finding the right user distribution, and lengthening horizon. Unless OpenAI and Anthropic find a new paradigm, the pace of progress on the China side won't differ much in the near term. On distillation: if US labs stop releasing or slow down sharply, will Chinese progress slow? Nathan thinks that would take a long time to show up.

points.h: Chinese open weights now lag by three weeks
points.body: Jordan observes that the open-weights part of Chinese models has slowed: first release in their own products and APIs, weights out two to three weeks later. Both Kimi and ZAI announced models first and uploaded weights to Hugging Face almost exactly three weeks later. He isn't sure whether this is an internal regulatory process — all Chinese AI labs have to communicate with the government and register releases — but finds the coincidence too strange. Nathan adds: this industry has historically had no tradition of giving release partners lots of extra time; usually it's "here's the model, hot potato, good luck," so if you really can get weights weeks in advance, that itself is a signal.

terms.def: Neither pause nor slowdown; implies still moving forward but controlling the tempo — criticized as an unmeasurable, self-interested framing.
Recursive self-improvement: a model improving itself, held to be the reason every capability not on that path gets ignored.
Publishing model parameters for public download; Chinese labs recently switched to shipping the product first and releasing weights two to three weeks later.
Improving continuously within the existing paradigm via tuning and scaling environments, rather than switching paradigms.

Time for frontier capabilities to diffuse to multiple organizations
facts.v: 3 to 6 months later 3 models can do it, a year later 20-plus organizations can do it
